questions.q: In the cotton route, which step removes the short fibres and makes the rest parallel?
questions.feedback: Combing removes the short fibres (noil) and lines up the rest. It is used only for combed yarn.

questions.q: Which step is needed for ring spinning but not for rotor spinning?
questions.feedback: The rotor takes sliver directly, so rotor spinning needs no roving. Ring spinning needs roving.

questions.q: What does compact spinning add to ring spinning?
options: A rotor instead of a ring
Suction that gathers the fibres into a tight bundle before twisting
A swirling air jet that twists the yarn
questions.feedback: Suction condenses the fibres just before the twist goes in, so compact yarn is less hairy, stronger and more lustrous.

questions.q: In ring spinning, what puts the twist into the yarn?
options: The traveller running round the ring as the bobbin turns
The groove inside a fast-spinning rotor
The leather tapes on the card
questions.feedback: The yarn runs through the traveller, which runs round the ring as the bobbin turns; each turn adds twist.

questions.q: Which extra step does the wool route add at the very start?
questions.feedback: Scouring washes the grease, dirt and sweat out of the fleece before carding.

questions.q: Most single yarns are spun with S twist and then plied with Z twist.
questions.feedback: False. Most singles are Z twist, and plying usually uses the opposite S twist to balance the yarn.

questions.q: In the English cotton count (Ne), what does a higher number mean?
questions.feedback: Ne counts 840-yard hanks per pound, so a higher number means a finer yarn.

questions.q: A yarn is written as 2/40s Ne. What is it?
options: Two Ne 40 singles plied, roughly as thick as Ne 20
An Ne 40 yarn with two turns per inch
A two-fibre blend spun at Ne 40
questions.feedback: The number before the slash is the number of plies: two Ne 40 singles give a yarn about as thick as Ne 20.

questions.q: What happens when a yarn gets more twist than its optimum?
options: The fibres shear, so it weakens and feels harsh
questions.feedback: Past the optimum, fibres shear against each other: the yarn weakens and becomes harsh and lively.

questions.q: A yarn test report shows a high CV%. What is a buyer most likely to see in the fabric?
questions.feedback: CV% measures variation in thickness along the yarn; high variation shows up as streaks.

questions.q: What is usually the biggest single cost in a yarn?
questions.feedback: Fibre is usually the biggest single cost, which is why expensive fibres are often blended with cheaper ones.

questions.q: Tex is a direct system: a higher tex number means a heavier, coarser yarn.
questions.feedback: True. Tex is grams per 1,000 metres, so a higher number means a coarser yarn, unlike Ne and Nm.

options: Fibres mixed before spinning, so each loses its identity in the yarn
Yarns of different fibres woven or knitted together
A yarn dyed in two colours
A fabric with a cotton face and a polyester back
questions.feedback: In an intimate blend the fibres are mixed before spinning, as in a 90/10 merino-nylon sock yarn.

questions.q: Why is cashmere often blended with wool?
questions.feedback: A cheaper fibre such as wool brings down the price of an expensive one such as cashmere.

questions.q: How does a grey marl (mélange) sweatshirt get its speckled look?
options: The yarn is dyed in sections
Fibres dyed different shades are blended before spinning
A coating is applied to the fabric
questions.feedback: Mélange comes from blending fibres of different shades before spinning.

questions.q: For most yarns, where is the largest environmental footprint?
options: In winding the yarn onto cones
Upstream, in growing or making the fibre
questions.feedback: Spinning mainly uses electricity; for most yarns the bigger footprint lies in growing or making the fibre.

questions.q: Which of these schemes certify recycled content? (Select all that apply.)
questions.feedback: GRS and RCS cover recycled content. RWS covers wool welfare, and GOTS covers organic textiles.

questions.q: Blended yarns are easier to recycle fibre-to-fibre than pure yarns.
questions.feedback: False. The fibres in a blend must be separated again, so blends are harder to recycle.
